The Zero-Punisher Testissue #226
Artificial humans · public goods game

Is the optimized stack still exploitable by never punishing?

The autoresearch campaign set out to fix a stack that rewarded doing nothing. This is the check of whether it worked.

Why the campaign

The artificial human stack (contribution, switch, punishment) was exploitable by a no-punishment policy, which kept RL training from finding intelligible policies other than "don't punish". This was documented with head-to-head matchups between the AH manager and the k-parameterized rule-based manager, above all the rule-based manager at different leniencies: none of them could beat the zero-punishment dummy on our win rate.

Our win rate

In each episode, the group whose payoff summed over its members, averaged over the 24 rounds, is higher wins; the win rate is the share of episodes won.

The claim to test

In our last meeting with Levin it was said that the optimized stack is no longer exploitable, so we set out to prove it. With our win rate we could not. See the win rates →

The models behind the artificial humans

The final stack

Five ways to call a winner

Baselines
zeronever punishesp = 0
AHclone of the human manager0–30
Decay rules · #99
p = ⌊(20 − c − t) / k⌋
k1harshestup to 20
k2up to 10
k4up to 5
k8most lenientup to 2
Levin's sigmoid rules · #219
Both zigzag in 4-round blocks: full strength right after a reshuffle, near 0 on the round a player may switch, since punishing a player who then leaves buys the group nothing.
optpunishes c ≤ 7; hardest in the first rounds, almost gone after round 12up to 30
cap10punishes c ≤ 9; fades evenly over the episodeup to 9
c = the player's contribution this round (0–20), t = round (0–23), p = the punishment the manager deals (0–30). Every rule punishes low contributors; the decay and sigmoid rules also punish less as the episode runs out.

Levin's definition for wins was different.

Score per group
pool = 1.6·Σc − Σp
  • Per round, empty group = 0; averaged over the episode
  • Each manager plays against the AH manager
  • Its group is compared with zero's group against AH, from a separate run
  • Decision: mean margin, 95% bootstrap interval over episodes
Who is compared
run AruleAH
run BzeroAH
The rule and zero never meet: each is scored against AH, and the two scores are compared.

Its weakness: it only compares how different strategies do against the AH model and picks the winner by who did better against it, so there are no head-to-heads.

Reading

With 1000 episodes per pairing, this definition does name winners: opt clearly, cap10 and k4 narrowly, while AH loses. They win only against the AH model; head to head (definition 5), none of them beats zero.

Score per group
pool = 1.6·Σc − Σp
  • Per round, empty group = 0; averaged over the episode
  • The manager's group against the zero group in the same episode, paired
  • Decision: win % and mean margin, 95% bootstrap interval
Who is compared
one runrulezero
The two managers share the world and the players who move between them.
Reading

Head to head with margins, AH and the decay rules k1–k4 lose to zero; k8 and Levin's sigmoid rules come closest but don't beat it.
